paper_title: StateWeaver: Multi-Agent Coordination of Story-State Transitions for Long-Horizon Video Generation

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Modern video foundation models generate high-quality short clips, but preserving long-video consistency and correctly depicting event-driven state changes remain challenging. Existing agentic workflows face these challenges because continual planning and repair accumulate context, while reference updates remain limited. We introduce StateWeaver, which combines Active States and Hierarchical Collaboration to connect review-driven visual reference updates with cross-shot state inheritance. Active States translate state discrepancies identified during review into concrete visual asset requirements that guide reference construction, validation, and regeneration, preserving identity and already-correct content while repairing target attributes. Confirmed generation results are linked to the corresponding asset states, story time, and reference versions for verification and reuse by subsequent shots. Hierarchical Collaboration isolates execution contexts by task, clip, and repair round, and uses hierarchical memory to organize this process across multiple sets. Across multiple benchmarks, StateWeaver outperforms existing methods and produces long videos with sustained cross-shot consistency under predefined and autonomously planned storyboards.

Existing agentic workflows face these challenges because continual planning and repair accumulate context, while reference updates remain limited. We introduce StateWeaver, which combines Active States and Hierarchical Collaboration to connect review-driven visual reference updates with cross-shot state inheritance. Active States translate state discrepancies identified during review into concrete visual asset requirements that guide reference construction, validation, and regeneration, preserving identity and already-correct content while repairing target attributes. Across multiple benchmarks, StateWeaver outperforms existing methods and produces long videos with sustained cross-shot consistency under predefined and autonomously planned storyboards. 1. Introduction Rapid advances in video foundation models have made highquality short-clip generation increasingly mature [11, 55, 70], while filmmaking, short-drama production, and embodied simulation demand long-horizon videos [9]. Existing production platforms organize clip generation through editable workflows [50, 63], but provide limited support for using generation feedback to coordinate corrections across shots. Local edits may therefore fail to preserve state continuity in subsequent clips and overall video coherence. Native long-video models face challenges in preserving quality and controlling error accumulation over extended generation horizons [8, 94, 98, 102]. Using short-clip foundation inheritance of repaired states. Building on existing explicit state representations, we propose Active States to plan asset changes from established story events and translate discrepancies identified in actual generation and review into concrete visual asset requirements. The system uses these requirements to construct and validate new visual conditions for targeted regeneration, preserving asset identity and already-correct content while repairing target attributes. Confirmed generation results are linked to the corresponding asset states, story time, and reference versions and update hierarchical memory, enabling subsequent shots to verify and reuse the changes realized through repair. Inspired by real-world filmmaking, we use Hierarchical Collaboration to organize continuous sub-stories as independent sets and isolate execution contexts by specialized task, clip planning, and repair round. Hierarchical memory persistently stores production records, allowing agents to recover relevant plans, references, and confirmed observations when switching tasks. Sets coordinate state handoffs through evidence dependencies. This organization connects the information needed for local repair with shared production information across sets, supporting autonomous iteration within each set and parallel execution of independent tasks. We conduct comparative evaluations on multiple videogeneration benchmarks [5, 16, 25, 101]. The results show that StateWeaver outperforms existing frameworks and generates long videos that maintain cross-shot consistency under both predefined and autonomously planned storyboards. Component ablations further demonstrate the contributions of state refinement and reference supplementation to state transitions and of context isolation to continual production. Our contributions are summarized as follows. We propose Active States to translate discrepancies found during review into state-refinement and visual-reference supplementation requirements, linking confirmed outputs to asset states and story time for targeted repair. We propose Hierarchical Collaboration to isolate execution contexts by task, clip, and repair round, retrieve relevant information through hierarchical memory, and coordinate evidence-based state handoffs across sets for continual planning, local repair, and parallel production. Results on four benchmarks show that StateWeaver improves long-video consistency under both predefined and autonomously planned storyboards, with human evaluation and ablations further validating the core mechanisms. 2. Related Work Video Generation. Modern video foundation models such as Seedance [11], Wan [70], and MiniMax H3 [55] improve generation through large-scale video training and can produce short clips with high visual fidelity and motion quality. Early temporal co-denoising and streaming memory provide Figure 2. Three paradigms of agentic long-video production. models as renderers, with agents autonomously coordinating planning, generation, and repair, offers promising route to combining visual quality, narrative continuity, and production automation [74, 90, 99]. As shown in Fig. 2, early agentic long-video frameworks use specialized roles [75, 91, 107] for planning [17, 20, 43], asset generation, and assembly, but their predefined plans [19, 84, 88] can allow uncorrected generation errors to propagate into subsequent shots. With advances in multimodal large language models [22, 48, 66, 67], MUSE [68] and CineCrew [6] incorporate review feedback into production decisions [41, 42, 83]. StoryEngine [81] and ATAS [78] further organize event-induced asset changes and validated observations through explicit states and temporal memory. These advances support dynamic planning [46, 82], statebased collaboration [26, 33, 112], and historical state reuse. However, continual production across multiple sub-stories requires coordinating task-specific execution contexts and visual conditions for new states. Specifically, explicitly recording target states before and after an event does not ensure that video realizes the intended change. Continual production needs to connect three steps. First, review findings must identify the visual conditions missing from current references and guide the construction of targeted references. Second, the state realized after regeneration must be confirmed so that subsequent shots inherit the repair instead of continuing to use outdated visual conditions. Finally, as these operations recur across tasks and sub-stories, local execution contexts need to be isolated while sharing state evidence relevant to the current story interval [44]. Local visual repair and subsequent coherent production thus need to be addressed jointly. We therefore introduce StateWeaver (as shown in Fig. 1), multi-agent framework for continual long-video production that connects review-driven visual updates with the Figure 3. Overview of StateWeaver. Active States support state planning, review-driven refinement, and reference supplementation, with confirmed results updating memory to preserve continuity across sets. Hierarchical Collaboration organizes the chief director, executive directors, and set directors, connecting isolated execution contexts through hierarchical story and asset memory. reusable mechanisms for extending clip generation [18, 73]. Coherent long videos, however, require contextual state to propagate across generation windows through temporal extension mechanisms [32, 51, 60, 69, 106] and explicit context management [3, 37, 95]. Recent methods learn sustained generation through hierarchical generation and transition modeling [7, 96, 105], long-context conditioning [14, 80], and autoregressive rollout [4, 27, 64]. JoyAI-Echo-1.5 [9] couples cross-shot audio-visual memory with rollout-aware training for persistent stories and interactive worlds. Long rollouts still degrade continuity and short-clip quality [8, 94]. Long-form and Agentic Video Generation. Agentic long-video frameworks organize short-clip generation into planning-to-assembly workflows [19, 88], drawing on story visualization [12, 38, 45, 58, 62] and storyboard planning [49, 111]. Reference conditioning [24, 71, 72, 104] and subject consistency control [15, 52, 77, 93, 109] preserve entity appearance, while multi-shot models [30, 53, 59, 76, 85] and visual memory [1, 21, 29, 36, 101, 108] provide reusable cross-shot context. Among the methods compared in this work, MovieAgent [84] uses staged planning and assembly, ViMax [25] follows fixed planning workflow, and StoryEngine [81] and ATAS [78] incorporate explicit states into generation. Related work extends staged and fixedplan production [23, 56, 86, 103] through multi-candidate selection [65], iterative feedback [35, 68, 100], and adaptive planning [6]. Further advances include compact context allocation [44], verification of extracted visual memories [34], persistent state tracking [26, 97], inference of subsequent entity states [2, 54, 110], and targeted visual repair [10, 13]. However, sustained production still faces two connected challenges: retaining relevant context across repeated planning and repair, and reliably propagating corrected visual observations across shots. Successful local repair alone does not ensure correct downstream reuse, which also depends on matching story intervals, asset states, source versions, and the scope under which each observation was verified. 3. StateWeaver organizes events and their story time from the screenplay, recording them separately from playback order and generation or repair rounds. The chief director first specifies base asset states and set entry and exit requirements, then establishes initial plans for states with concrete reference purposes and refines or supplements states and references according to shot requirements and review feedback. StateWeaver defines local production scopes by sets, organizes temporary execution contexts by specialized task, clip, and repair round, and recovers production information from persistent memory. The chief director oversees planning, task assignment, and cross-set scheduling, delegating asset preparation, repair diagnosis, candidate reassessment, and blocked-task handling to executive directors. Task-context isolation (TCI) creates an independent context for each specialized task to read task requirements and relevant evidence, return conclusions and evidence pointers, and release the context upon completion. Set directors apply clipand repair-round planning-context isolation (CCI), starting new planning context when switching clips or beginning new repair round. Each context reads the current plan, applicable references, confirmed observations, and relevant repair decisions. Complete conversations from the preceding task or round are not automatically carried over. Formal self-review uses an independent candidate-review context [89], with review results read by the next planning round. The chief director reads specialized reports and unresolved issues on demand, persistently recording scheduling decisions and resumption points for later coordination. Hierarchical Story and Asset Memory. StateWeaver uses global memory MG for story facts, asset information, and confirmed observations shared across sets, and set memory MS for local plans, generated observations, and repair decisions. Both levels comprise story memory and asset memory, respectively organizing character relationships, event order, and goal changes, and visual materials and their provenance indexed by asset, story state, and reference version. Entries record applicable events, clips, and story intervals, distinguishing planned facts, target references, and actual observations. The system first restricts entries to accessible records with valid sources, then applies memory scope filtering (SF) by event and story interval. Agents read task-relevant plans, references, and preceding evidence from these results and expand detailed records on demand. GPT-Image-2.5-Sunburst generates or edits visual references, and MiniMax-H3-Sol [55] generates videos from prompts and reference images in Ref2VA mode. We construct an evaluation suite of 75 text-driven video production tasks from ST-Bench [101], ViMax-Bench [25], EntityBench [16], and DirectorBench [5], and compare StateWeaver with MovieAgent [84], ViMax [25], StoryEngine [81], and ATAS [78]. Ablation Analysis We conduct ablation experiments on DirectorBench to evaluate the role of each key component of StateWeaver. Each ablation variant removes or disables only the components under investigation, while all other modules and experimental settings remain identical to those of the full StateWeaver framework, ensuring fair comparison. sections.content: A. Overview In this appendix, we explain how StateWeaver records event completion and visible asset states separately, traces the reference images submitted for repair, and links specific observations in source frame to the reference revisions used by the next set. For reproducibility, we detail deployment and the automated and blind human evaluations on all four benchmarks under their respective storyboard settings. We then present more representative examples and several failure cases. Benchmark Composition and Task Selection We selected 75 production tasks from four benchmarks, using the story as the unit of selection. For benchmarks with predefined storyboards, we used the original scripts to select stories that vary in how shots change, how many scenes they span, and how characters interact. For autonomous storyboarding, we first identified briefs that leave shot planning to the framework, then selected briefs covering different types of production. All five frameworks received the same 50 tasks with predefined storyboards and 25 tasks requiring autonomous planning. We report task counts by benchmark in Tab. D.1 and list each tasks original benchmark identifier in Tab. D.2. ST-Bench [101]. We selected 20 of the 30 original scripts, considering story genre, changes in viewpoint and setting, and interactions between characters and props. Each selected story contains 712 shots. We retained the original shot order and cut or continuation markers to assess whether characters and props remain recognizable when shot scale or viewpoint changes, and whether an action marked as continuous carries naturally from one shot to the next. ViMax-Bench [25]. We selected 20 of the 35 stories across the benchmarks three consistency categories, with six stories testing character persistence (Type A), six testing background persistence (Type B), and eight testing multicharacter interaction (Type C). Each category places different demand on cross-shot generation. gardener appearing across four seasons must remain recognizable as the surroundings change. board game tournament held in single cafe requires the spatial layout to remain consistent across camera positions. In band rehearsal, the performers must remain distinguishable both when shown in alternating shots and when playing together. EntityBench [16]. We grouped the 140 candidate clips by source story, kept one clip per source, and selected 10 scripts based on the benchmarks difficulty labels and sequence lengths. The six medium-difficulty scripts contain 1522 shots each, and the four hard scripts contain 50 shots each. We checked the shot boundaries used for continuity evaluation against the actions specified for each shot, the scheduled appearances of entities, and the cut markers. When choosing replacements, we excluded scripts that explicitly called for depictions of graphic injury. This range of sequence lengths lets us assess both continuity between adjacent shots and the consistency of characters, props, or locations that reappear after several intervening shots. DirectorBench [5]. We reviewed all 75 original production briefs individually and identified 33 that support autonomous shot planning from text alone. We excluded briefs that depend on external images, already specify multiple shots in detail, explicitly require an animation style, or request only still image. We retained individual cameramovement or visual requirements when they constrain what appears on screen while leaving the framework free to decide how to divide the sequence into shots and arrange them. From these candidates, we selected 25 briefs based on production type and duration requirements, limiting overlap among similar tasks. The selection covers eight categories spanning action, cinematography, commercial marketing, education and news, music, narrative, science fiction, and everyday vlogs. D.2. On DirectorBench, each framework plans the shot content and order from the same brief. Each task includes the story, visual requirements, and any explicit duration constraints. Five raters from the same group independently judge each pair blind. Each reads the fixed story brief, watches both muted videos in full, and judges three dimensions separately. As shown in Fig. D.1, we label the two videos and for blind evaluation. keyed hash of the rater and pair identifiers determines the leftright order, which stays the same on repeat visit. Cross-shot continuity assesses whether characters, props, and scenes remain coherent across cuts. State transition assesses whether key changes occur and persist in later shots. Visual quality covers overall clarity, motion, and visible artifacts. Predefined Storyboards The ST-Bench painting storyboard calls for cut from close-up of the artist applying paint to wide shot of the easel. In the enlarged regions of Fig. E.1, the flat brush leaves new stroke with hooked upper end to the left of an existing blue patch. Both the hook and its position relative to the patch remain recognizable in the wide shot. Across this change in shot scale, StateWeaver preserves both the new detail introduced by the brushstroke and the existing appearance of the canvas. E.2. Autonomous Storyboard Planning In the DirectorBench folk performance in Fig. E.2, StateWeaver plans the shots in which the singer moves scarf and resumes playing. The singer lifts the folded scarf from the chair seat and drapes it over the wooden backrest. When the singer returns hand to the guitar, the fringe still hangs below the back rail. This detail shows how StateWeaver preserves the prop state established by an earlier action even as the autonomously planned sequence shifts attention back to the performance. E.3. The subsequent sanding shot uses the final frame of this candidate as local reference, and the board markings remain visible beside the sandpaper. In this way, StateWeaver reuses the board appearance and pencil mark verified during local repair while retaining record of camera drift in the candidate selected as compromise. The accuracy of the measurement cannot be verified from these frames. E.4. For entities depicted in the reference materials, StateWeaver maintains continuity across changes in viewpoint or setting. For example, the pink paper flower and the cylindrical instrument remain recognizable from different angles (a, d). The same gardener appears in the vegetable garden in different seasons, and the same chess player can be identified in reverse shot (c, e). Before filming, they could compare the two versions to see which better conveys the change in the relationship. This could reduce the cost of repeated test shoots for independent filmmakers and small teams. Film students could also compare versions of the same script to see how shot choices shape viewers interpretations of story.
